entries.patterns: adjure + sb + to-infinitive / adjure + sb + that-clause (archaic) / adjure + sb + by + noun phrase (adjured him by all he held sacred)
entries.never: adjure someone from doing something / adjure to do something
entries.meaning: A command laid on someone under oath or in the name of something sacred — it sits between command and implore and carries an appeal to conscience that neither of its neighbors has. Unlike a plain order, it presumes the hearer wants to do right.
entries.transform: "In the name of everything you believe in, tell me the truth." -> He adjured me to tell the truth.
examples: The witness was adjured to answer truthfully or not at all.
He adjured them to remember what the founders had risked.
The high priest adjured him to say whether the charge was true.
In the last paragraph she adjures her readers to check the primary sources themselves.
Nobody had adjured me to secrecy; I simply kept quiet.
She adjured him by the memory of his mother not to sell the farm.

entries.patterns: allow + sb + to-infinitive / allow + -ing (no person named: allows smoking) / allow + noun phrase / allow + sb + noun phrase (allowed us ten minutes) / passive be allowed to (very common) / allow for + noun phrase (= make room for, a different verb: allow for traffic) / allow + that-clause (a different verb — see below)
entries.never: allow that you park here / allow someone doing something
entries.meaning: Permission as the withdrawal of an objection — weaker than permit, which is institutional, and than authorize, which requires someone with formal power. Its negative is the everyday way English forbids things: They don't allow dogs in here.
entries.transform: "You can use my car." -> She allowed me to use her car.
examples: My parents never allowed us to eat in the living room.
The airline allows one carry-on and one personal item.
Her visa allowed her to stay another ninety days.
The building doesn't allow subletting under any circumstances.
The judge allowed the question, over the objection.
I'll allow that the timing looks bad, but nothing was hidden.

entries.patterns: appeal to + sb + to-infinitive / appeal to + sb + for + noun phrase / appeal for + noun phrase (no addressee named) / appeal to + sb (bare: appealed to the crowd)
entries.never: appeal someone to do something
entries.meaning: An urgent request broadcast to people who are under no obligation to comply — the verb of press conferences, open letters, and relief campaigns. It has no authority behind it at all, which is exactly what distinguishes it from demand and call on.
entries.transform: "If anyone saw anything that night, please come forward." -> Police appealed to witnesses to come forward.
examples: The mayor appealed to residents to conserve water through the weekend.
Aid groups have appealed for another forty million dollars.
She appealed to her brother for help with the mortgage.
Both sides appealed to the union to return to the table.
He appealed to the crowd's better instincts and got nowhere.
The family appealed to anyone with information to call the tip line.

entries.type: reporting verb — request (also the neutral question verb)
entries.patterns: ask + sb + to-infinitive / ask + to-infinitive (the subject acts) / ask + (sb) + for + noun phrase / ask + that-clause (subjunctive; formal) / ask + sb + wh-clause / ask + sb + if/whether-clause / ask + sb + noun phrase (asked me a question) / ask + sb + about + noun phrase
entries.never: ask to someone to do something / ask for to do something
entries.meaning: The unmarked request — neutral in force, neutral in register, and silent about how politely the original was phrased. "Close the window," "Could you close the window?" and "I hate to ask, but would it be possible to close the window?" all come out as She asked me to close the window; if the manner mattered, use an adverb or a stronger verb.
entries.transform: "Could you close the window?" -> She asked me to close the window.
examples: He asked me to water his plants while he was in Tulsa.
She asked to speak to whoever was in charge.
I asked the waiter for a glass of tap water.
We ask that all phones be silenced during the performance.
Nobody asked him to do any of this.
She asked whether the position was still open.

entries.patterns: authorize + sb + to-infinitive / authorize + noun phrase (authorized the payment) / passive be authorized to (very common)
entries.never: authorize to release the funds / authorize someone doing something
entries.meaning: Permission conferred by someone whose office gives them the power to confer it. allow removes an objection; authorize creates a right, and it implies a record — a signature, a resolution, a memo. Its passive is where it lives: You are not authorized to be in this room.
entries.transform: "You may release the funds." -> The board authorized us to release the funds.
examples: Congress authorized the agency to issue subpoenas.
Only two people are authorized to sign checks over ten thousand dollars.
Her supervisor authorized the overtime in writing.
Nobody authorized this purchase, and now it's on the audit.
The warrant authorized them to search the garage but not the house.
I'm not authorized to discuss an open investigation.

entries.patterns: ban + noun phrase / ban + -ing / ban + sb + from + -ing / ban + sb + from + noun phrase (banned him from the building)
entries.never: ban someone to do something
entries.meaning: The suppression of an activity by a government, an institution, or a governing body — the activity is the target, and the people affected are whoever happens to be doing it. Contrast bar, which targets a person, and forbid, which is what one person says to another.
entries.transform: "No one may fly drones in the park." -> The city banned drones from the park.
examples: Several states have banned the sale of flavored vaping products.
The league banned him for the rest of the season.
Our building banned smoking on the balconies in 2019.
The country banned imports of beef from three provinces.
She was banned from the online forum for a week.
You can't ban a book from a public library that easily.

entries.patterns: bar + sb + from + -ing / bar + sb + from + noun phrase / bar + noun phrase (legal: the statute bars recovery)
entries.never: bar someone to do something / bar someone doing something
entries.meaning: Prohibition achieved by shutting someone out — of a place, an office, a profession, a remedy. ban abolishes an activity; bar excludes a person from it. In legal writing it is also the verb for a rule that forecloses a claim: The statute of limitations bars the suit.
entries.transform: "You are not to enter the courtroom." -> The judge barred him from entering the courtroom.
examples: The state barred him from practicing medicine for five years.
Security barred us from the loading dock without a badge.
A conflict of interest bars her from voting on the measure.
Nothing in the lease bars tenants from keeping a cat.
The court held that the settlement barred any further claims.
He was barred from the building the same afternoon he was fired.

entries.patterns: beg + sb + to-infinitive / beg + to-infinitive (the subject acts) / beg + (sb) + for + noun phrase / beg + of + sb (formal and dated: I beg of you) / beg + that-clause (subjunctive; literary)
entries.never: beg to someone to do something
entries.meaning: A request made from need, with the speaker's dignity spent — the bottom of the force scale. Reporting a request as begged is a strong editorial claim about the original: it says the speaker had no leverage.
entries.transform: "Please, please don't tell him." -> She begged me not to tell him.
examples: She begged her landlord to hold the apartment until Friday.
He begged to be excused from the table.
The dog begs for scraps every single night.
I begged him not to put it in writing.
They begged the committee for one more hearing.
I beg to differ with almost everything in that paragraph.

entries.patterns: beseech + sb + to-infinitive / beseech + sb + for + noun phrase / beseech + that-clause (archaic)
entries.never: beseech to someone / beseech someone doing something
entries.meaning: An urgent, humbled plea — beg transposed into a liturgical or high-literary key. Almost nobody uses it of an ordinary conversation; using it of one is a deliberate exaggeration.
entries.transform: "I implore you — spare the city." -> He besought them to spare the city.
examples: She beseeched the governor to grant a stay of execution.
In the letter he besought his brother for forgiveness.
We beseech thee, O Lord, to look upon this house.
The ambassador beseeched both capitals to keep the line open.
I beseeched him — half joking, half not — to stop sending me drafts at midnight.
The petition beseeches the council to reconsider the closure.

entries.patterns: bid + sb + bare infinitive (bade her enter) / bid + sb + to-infinitive (older and rarer) / bid + sb + noun phrase (bade them farewell)
entries.never: bid that she leave / bid to someone to do something
entries.meaning: A command in a raised, old-fashioned register — the verb of scripture, fairy tales, and historical fiction. In everyday American English it survives mainly in bid farewell and do as you're bidden.
entries.transform: "Come in." -> He bade her enter.
examples: The king bade the messenger rise.
She bade us farewell at the platform and did not look back.
He did as he was bidden and asked no questions.
The innkeeper bade them come in out of the rain.
Custom bids us wait until the eldest is seated.
I bid you good night.

entries.patterns: call on + sb + to-infinitive / call on + sb + for + noun phrase / call for + noun phrase (no addressee: called for calm) / call for + -ing (called for tightening the rules)
entries.never: call someone to resign / call on someone doing something
entries.meaning: A demand made in public, addressed to someone with the power to act, by someone with no power to compel them. It is the standard verb of resolutions, statements, and editorials. Call upon is the same verb, one register higher.
entries.transform: "The minister must resign." -> The opposition called on the minister to resign.
examples: Three senators called on the agency to release the full report.
The union called for a strike vote by the end of the month.
She called upon her colleagues to put the vote off a week.
The editorial calls on the mayor to apologize publicly.
Nobody called for his resignation, but nobody defended him either.
He called on us for a decision before the market opened.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal instruction assigning a duty
entries.patterns: charge + sb + to-infinitive / charge + sb + with + -ing (charged him with organizing the drive) / charge + sb + with + noun phrase / passive be charged with (the commonest form) / charge + that-clause (a different verb — see below)
entries.never: charge someone that they do something / charge someone to do something
entries.meaning: A solemn instruction that hands somebody a responsibility — a judge to a jury, an outgoing officer to a successor, a commencement speaker to a graduating class. It is instruct with ceremony attached.
entries.transform: "Consider only the evidence you heard in this room." -> The judge charged the jury to consider only the evidence.
examples: The judge charged the jurors to disregard the last exchange entirely.
The commission was charged with reviewing every permit issued since 2020.
He charged his successor to finish what the department had started.
She charged us to keep the news to ourselves until Monday.
The task force is charged with producing recommendations by spring.
In his last letter he charged them to look after their mother.

entries.patterns: command + sb + to-infinitive / command + that-clause (subjunctive) / command + noun phrase (commanded silence)
entries.never: command to advance / command that he advances
entries.meaning: The strongest directive in the language — an order from someone whose authority makes refusal a breach of duty. Where order is administrative and can come from a doctor or a court, command is military, royal, or divine, and in ordinary American office English it always sounds like an exaggeration.
entries.transform: "Fall back to the ridge." -> The general commanded them to fall back to the ridge.
examples: The captain commanded the crew to stand down.
She commanded him to leave the house and never come back.
The statute commands that every ballot be preserved for twenty-two months.
He does not so much ask as command.
Her work commands respect even from people who disagree with it.
The officer commanded us not to move until the all-clear.

entries.patterns: decree + that-clause (subjunctive) / decree + noun phrase (decreed a general amnesty)
entries.never: decree someone to do something
entries.meaning: A command that becomes law the instant it is uttered, issued by an authority answerable to no one. Applied to an ordinary person it is heavily ironic — My sister has decreed that we're doing Thanksgiving at her place.
entries.transform: "All shops will close on Sunday." -> The governor decreed that all shops close on Sunday.
examples: The czar decreed that the calendar be changed.
The court decreed that the estate be divided equally among the three children.
Some committee somewhere has decreed that we all use the new template.
In 1685 the king decreed the revocation of the edict.
Nature has not decreed that offices must be cold.
The board decreed that no exceptions be made for anyone.

entries.patterns: demand + that-clause (subjunctive) / demand + to-infinitive (the subject acts: demanded to see the manager) / demand + noun phrase / demand + noun phrase + of + sb (demanded an explanation of him) / demand + of + sb + that-clause (formal)
entries.never: demand someone to do something
entries.meaning: A request presented as an entitlement, with no room left for a no. It differs from require in that a person demands and a rule requires, and from insist on in that demand is a single act while insist implies repetition against resistance.
entries.transform: "I want to see the manager, right now." -> She demanded to see the manager.
examples: The union demanded that the layoffs be rescinded.
He demanded to know who had authorized the transfer.
Protesters demanded the release of the detained journalists.
She demanded of him an explanation he was in no position to give.
The tenants demanded that the heat be fixed before the weekend.
Nobody is demanding perfection; we're asking for a deadline.

entries.patterns: dictate + that-clause / dictate + noun phrase (dictated the terms) / dictate + noun phrase + to + sb (dictated the terms to them) / dictate + wh-clause (dictates who gets in) / dictate to + sb (intransitive: nobody dictates to me)
entries.never: dictate someone to do something
entries.meaning: Terms laid down by whoever is in a position to lay them down, with an unmistakable note of resentment on the reporter's part. Nobody describes their own reasonable instruction as dictating.
entries.transform: "You'll hire whoever I tell you to hire." -> He dictated who they would hire.
examples: The larger firm dictated every clause of the merger agreement.
Policy dictates that all incidents be logged within twenty-four hours.
He isn't going to let a subcontractor dictate to him.
Weather dictated the schedule more than anything on the whiteboard did.
The budget dictates how many people we can bring on this year.
She dictated two letters and a memo before nine.

entries.patterns: direct + sb + to-infinitive / direct + that-clause (subjunctive) / direct + sb + to + noun phrase (a different sense: directed us to the elevators)
entries.never: direct someone doing something / direct to do something
entries.meaning: An instruction issued through a chain of authority — the verb of court orders, agency letters, and corporate memoranda. It has the force of order without its edge: nobody is being shouted at, but nobody is being asked either.
entries.transform: "Produce the documents by Friday." -> The court directed the company to produce the documents by Friday.
examples: The inspector directed us to shut the line down until the guard was replaced.
Her will directs that the proceeds go to the county library.
The memo directed all staff to complete the training by the fifteenth.
The referee directed both coaches to their benches.
He was directed to appear at ten and showed up at noon.
The statute directs the agency to publish its findings annually.

entries.patterns: enjoin + sb + to-infinitive (= order them to) / enjoin + sb + from + -ing (= forbid them from) / enjoin + that-clause (subjunctive) / enjoin + noun phrase (enjoined silence, enjoined the merger)
entries.never: enjoin someone doing something / enjoin someone against doing something
entries.meaning: In law, a binding order of a court, most often one that stops something. In older moral and religious writing, a duty solemnly urged.
entries.transform: "Stop selling the product immediately." -> The court enjoined the company from selling the product.
examples: A federal judge enjoined the state from enforcing the new rule.
The rule of the order enjoined silence between compline and dawn.
Plaintiffs asked the court to enjoin the merger pending review.
He was enjoined from contacting any former client for two years.
Scripture enjoins believers to care for the widow and the orphan.
The injunction enjoining construction was lifted in March.

entries.patterns: entreat + sb + to-infinitive / entreat + sb + for + noun phrase / entreat + that-clause (formal, rare)
entries.never: entreat to someone to do something / entreat someone from doing something
entries.meaning: An earnest and courteous plea — beg with the desperation removed and the manners left in. Where beg implies the speaker has nothing left, entreat implies only that they care very much. It is a written word; almost no American says it aloud.
entries.transform: "Please, I'm asking you to reconsider." -> She entreated him to reconsider.
examples: The letter entreats the governor to commute the sentence.
She entreated her son to write, even a postcard.
He entreated them for a few more days to find the money.
I entreat you to read the second half before you decide.
The delegation entreated both sides to keep talking.
His mother had entreated him not to enlist, and he enlisted anyway.

entries.patterns: exhort + sb + to-infinitive / exhort + sb + to + noun phrase (exhorted them to greater effort) / exhort + that-clause (subjunctive; rare)
entries.never: exhort someone doing something / exhort to someone
entries.meaning: Urging delivered as rhetoric, to an audience rather than to a person — the verb of sermons, locker rooms, and commencement addresses. It is urge with an intended crowd, and unlike order it carries no power to compel: an exhortation can simply be ignored.
entries.transform: "Leave nothing on the field out there." -> The coach exhorted them to leave nothing on the field.
examples: He exhorted the volunteers to knock on one more door before dark.
The general exhorted his troops to hold the line one more hour.
Her columns exhort readers to vote in local elections nobody follows.
The letter exhorts the churches to stand firm.
She exhorted us to greater discipline and, less usefully, to greater cheerfulness.
Coaches can exhort all they want; the roster is the roster.

entries.patterns: forbid + sb + to-infinitive / forbid + sb + from + -ing / forbid + -ing (no person named: forbids smoking) / forbid + noun phrase / forbid + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: forbid someone doing something
entries.meaning: A prohibition spoken by one person to another whom they have authority over — a parent, a boss, a commanding officer. Compare the institutional verbs:
entries.transform: "You may not enter the lab." -> She forbade us to enter the lab. / She forbade us from entering the lab.
examples: Her father forbade her to see him again, which settled the matter in the other direction.
The lease forbids subletting for periods under thirty days.
Doctrine forbids members from taking an oath of any kind.
The coach forbade us to talk to reporters before the hearing.
Nothing in the bylaws forbids a board member from also being a vendor.
God forbid anyone actually reads the terms of service.

entries.patterns: implore + sb + to-infinitive / implore + sb + for + noun phrase / implore + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: implore to someone to do something / implore someone from doing something
entries.meaning: The most emotionally charged of the pleading verbs — more intense than beg, less ritualized than beseech. It reports desperation without reporting loss of dignity, which is why journalists reach for it when quoting families of the missing.
entries.transform: "Please — please don't do this." -> He implored her not to do it.
examples: She implored the committee to hear one more witness.
His parents implored anyone who had seen the car to call the police.
I implore you to read the fine print this one time.
The doctor implored him to stop driving.
He implored her for a second chance and did not get one.
The letter implores the company not to close the last plant in the county.

entries.patterns: insist on + -ing / insist on + noun phrase / insist on + sb's + -ing (insisted on my paying) / insist on + sb + -ing (insisted on me paying — commoner in speech, still flagged by some editors) / bare insist + that-clause (subjunctive) / bare insist (intransitive: I insisted)
entries.never: insist someone to do something / insist on someone to do something
entries.meaning: A demand repeated against resistance. demand is a single act; insist implies the speaker has already been told no at least once and is not accepting it.
entries.transform: "No — I'm paying. I'm paying." -> He insisted on paying.
examples: She insisted on driving me to the airport at four in the morning.
He insisted on an itemized bill before he'd sign anything.
My grandmother insisted that everyone eat before the photographs.
They insisted on our being there an hour early, for no reason anyone explained.
The bank insists on two forms of identification.
He insisted that he had never met her, and the photographs said otherwise.

entries.patterns: instruct + sb + to-infinitive / instruct + that-clause (subjunctive) / instruct + sb + that-clause (informational) / instruct + sb + wh-clause (instructed us how to file it) / instruct + sb + in + noun phrase (= teach)
entries.never: instruct to fill out the form / instruct someone doing something
entries.meaning: A directive given as part of a procedure or a job — authority without emotion. A clerk instructs, a supervisor instructs, a lawyer instructs a client; none of them is angry. Compare tell, which is neutral but personal, and direct, which is one step more official.
entries.transform: "Fill out the form in blue ink." -> The clerk instructed us to fill out the form in blue ink.
examples: The flight attendant instructed passengers to stow all loose items.
Her attorney instructed her to answer only the question asked.
The manual instructs you to disconnect the battery first.
He instructed the desk that no calls were to be put through.
She instructed us in how the filing system had been organized, which took an hour.
The pharmacist instructed him not to take it on an empty stomach.

entries.patterns: let + sb + bare infinitive / let + sb + adverbial particle (let him in, let the dog out) / let's + bare infinitive (the first-person imperative)
entries.never: let someone to do something
entries.meaning: Permission in its most ordinary, domestic form — no institution, no paperwork, often no explicit request.
entries.transform: "You can borrow the car." -> She let me borrow the car.
examples: My parents never let me stay out past eleven.
Let me know when the car's out front.
She wouldn't let him pay for dinner.
They let the dog out at six every morning without fail.
He let the lease run out rather than argue about the deposit.
Don't let anyone tell you this was inevitable.

entries.type: reporting verb — legal or institutional requirement
entries.patterns: mandate + that-clause (subjunctive) / mandate + noun phrase (mandates helmets) / passive be mandated to + infinitive (institutional)
entries.never: the law mandates employers to provide coverage
entries.meaning: A requirement imposed by law, ordinance, or a governing body, on a whole class of people at once. Nobody mandates anything to an individual in conversation. Compare require, which is the same idea one register down and which happily takes the object plus infinitive.
entries.transform: "Every employee must complete the training." -> The policy mandates that every employee complete the training.
examples: Twenty-nine states mandate some form of paid sick leave.
The settlement mandates that the department publish quarterly data.
Federal law mandates a ninety-day notice period for plant closings.
The commission is mandated to report to the legislature each January.
Nothing in the charter mandates that meetings be held in person.
The district mandated masks for two weeks and then rescinded the rule.

entries.patterns: nag + sb + to-infinitive / nag + sb + about + noun phrase / nag + sb + into + -ing / nag at + sb / nag (intransitive)
entries.never: nag someone that they should do something / nag someone doing something
entries.meaning: Requesting so often that the repetition itself has become the problem — the only verb in this group whose meaning includes the listener's reaction rather than the speaker's force. Reporting a request as nagging is an editorial verdict, and one that has historically been aimed at women far more than at men, which is worth knowing before you choose it in writing about a real person.
entries.transform: "Have you called the dentist? Have you called the dentist yet?" -> She nagged me to call the dentist.
examples: My roommate nagged me to return the library books until I finally did.
She nagged him about the smoke detector for a year, and then it went off at 3 a.m.
He nagged his way into a corner office and a reputation.
Stop nagging — I'll do it after lunch.
Something about the second paragraph kept nagging at me.
They nagged the city into repaving the block.

entries.patterns: order + sb + to-infinitive / order + that-clause (subjunctive) / order + noun phrase (ordered a recount) / order + sb + adverbial particle (ordered him out)
entries.never: order to someone to do something / order that he leaves
entries.meaning: The default word for an authoritative directive. Broader than command, which is military or absolute, and colder than tell, which is the same act reported without ceremony. A court, a doctor, a captain, and a parent can all order; only the first three sound natural doing it in a report.
entries.transform: "Evacuate the building." -> The chief ordered us to evacuate the building.
examples: The captain ordered the crew to abandon ship.
Her doctor ordered her to stay off the ankle for six weeks.
The court ordered that the company turn over its internal emails.
He ordered us out of the kitchen before the smoke alarm went off.
The agency ordered a recall of every lot from that plant.
Nobody ordered me to be here; I volunteered.

entries.patterns: permit + sb + to-infinitive / permit + -ing (no person named: permits smoking) / permit + noun phrase / passive be permitted to (very common) / permit of + noun phrase (formal: permits of no exception)
entries.never: permit that employees park here
entries.meaning: Institutional permission, stated in policies and posted on signs. Between let (domestic), allow (general), and authorize (a conferred power), permit is the one that belongs to rules.
entries.transform: "Employees may park here after six." -> The building permits employees to park there after six.
examples: The permit permits excavation only between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m.
Her schedule doesn't permit a trip that long.
The museum does not permit flash photography in the print rooms.
Guests are permitted to use the pool until ten.
Weather permitting, the ceremony will be outdoors.
The evidence permits of no other reading.

entries.patterns: petition + sb + to-infinitive / petition + sb + for + noun phrase / petition for + noun phrase / petition + that-clause (subjunctive; legal)
entries.never: petition to the court to reopen the case
entries.meaning: A request put to an authority in the form the authority requires — signatures, a filing, a formal letter. It reports the document as much as the utterance, which is why it is nearly always in the past tense and about groups.
entries.transform: "We ask the court to reopen the case." -> They petitioned the court to reopen the case.
examples: Residents petitioned the council to put a stoplight at the intersection.
He petitioned the state for reinstatement of his license.
Nineteen faculty members petitioned the dean to reverse the decision.
She petitioned the court to seal the juvenile records.
The union petitioned that the vote be conducted by secret ballot.
You can petition for a hardship waiver, but almost nobody gets one.

entries.patterns: plead with + sb + to-infinitive / plead for + noun phrase / plead with + sb + for + noun phrase / plead + noun phrase (pleaded ignorance, pleaded guilty — different senses) / plead + that-clause (= argue, a different sense)
entries.never: plead someone to do something
entries.meaning: An appeal made over time and with visible emotion — longer than a beg, less formal than an appeal to. Note that the courtroom senses (plead guilty, plead the Fifth, plead a case) are separate verbs that report an entry on the record, not a request.
entries.transform: "Please, just hear me out." -> He pleaded with me to hear him out.
examples: She pleaded with her brother to see a doctor.
The family pleaded for privacy after the verdict.
He pleaded with the officer not to write the ticket.
Neighbors pleaded with the city to slow traffic on the street for years.
He pleaded guilty to two counts and got probation.
She pleaded ignorance, unconvincingly.

entries.patterns: press + sb + to-infinitive / press + sb + for + noun phrase / press + sb + on + noun phrase (pressed him on the timeline) / press for + noun phrase / press + noun phrase (pressed the point)
entries.never: press that someone do something / press someone doing something
entries.meaning: Persistent pushing toward an action or an answer, without the authority of order or the irritation of nag. It is the standard verb for a journalist who will not let a question go: Pressed on why the memo was never sent, she declined to answer.
entries.transform: "Come on — are you taking the job or not?" -> She pressed me to take the job.
examples: My advisor pressed me to submit before the fall deadline.
Reporters pressed the spokesman for a number and never got one.
The board is pressing for an outside audit.
She pressed him on the timeline until he admitted it had slipped.
They pressed us to sign that afternoon, which was itself a warning.
Nobody pressed the point, and the meeting moved on.

entries.patterns: prohibit + noun phrase / prohibit + -ing / prohibit + sb + from + -ing / prohibit + sb + from + noun phrase
entries.never: prohibit someone to do something
entries.meaning: Prohibition written into a rule, a statute, a policy, or a lease — the prohibiting is done by the document, and the person who wrote it has usually vanished from the sentence. Compare forbid, where a person forbids another person.
entries.transform: "Employees may not accept gifts." -> The policy prohibits employees from accepting gifts.
examples: Federal law prohibits airlines from denying boarding on those grounds.
The lease prohibits subletting without written consent.
Our code of conduct prohibits accepting anything worth more than twenty-five dollars.
The injunction prohibited him from coming within five hundred feet of the school.
Nothing prohibits a nonprofit from lobbying; it just limits how much.
The rule prohibits the use of personal email for agency business.

entries.patterns: prompt + sb + to-infinitive / prompt + noun phrase (prompted an investigation) / prompt + sb + for + noun phrase (prompted him for the password) / prompt + sb + with + noun phrase
entries.never: prompt someone that they should do something / prompt someone doing something
entries.meaning: The smallest directive in the file — one line, once, and only because the listener had stalled. An actor who forgets a line is prompted; so is a witness who needs the question repeated.
entries.transform: "Go on — tell them what you told me." -> She prompted me to repeat what I had told her.
examples: A whisper from the wings prompted him to pick up the line.
Her question prompted me to look at the numbers again.
The audit prompted a complete rewrite of the approval process.
The system prompts you for a second factor after ninety days.
He had to be prompted twice before he thanked anyone.
Nothing in the email prompted us to think it was urgent.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal condemnation and prohibition
entries.patterns: proscribe + noun phrase / proscribe + -ing
entries.never: proscribe someone to do something / proscribe someone from doing something
entries.meaning: A formal denunciation that also forbids — historically, outlawing a person; now, ruling a practice out of bounds. It is the verb of style guides, professional codes, and academic writing about norms.
entries.transform: "The passive voice is not to be used in these documents." -> The manual proscribes the passive voice.
examples: Most professional codes proscribe undisclosed conflicts of interest.
The regime proscribed the party and jailed its leadership.
Nothing in the guidelines proscribes citing preprints; they just discourage it.
Church law proscribed the practice for four centuries.
Grammar handbooks once proscribed the split infinitive, and nobody listened.
The treaty proscribes an entire class of weapon.

entries.patterns: push + sb + to-infinitive / push + sb + into + -ing / push for + noun phrase / push + sb + on + noun phrase
entries.never: push someone doing something / push that someone do something
entries.meaning: Repeated pressure toward a decision, with a strong hint that the person pushed was reluctant and the person pushing had an interest. It is press with the speaker's motives in view.
entries.transform: "You should really apply. Apply. Have you applied?" -> My advisor pushed me to apply.
examples: Her parents pushed her to take the safer offer.
Two members of the board have been pushing for a change at the top since March.
He pushed me into buying the extended warranty and I've regretted it since.
Don't push him on it tonight; wait until he's slept.
The agency is pushing utilities to publish outage data.
Nobody pushed me; I wanted to go.

entries.type: reporting verb — directive resting on prior intent
entries.patterns: remind + sb + to-infinitive / remind + sb + that-clause / remind + sb + of + noun phrase / remind + sb + about + noun phrase / remind + sb + wh-clause
entries.never: remind to bring your passport / remind someone doing something
entries.meaning: A directive whose whole force comes from the listener's own earlier intention — you can only be reminded to do something you had already meant to do. That presupposition is what separates it from tell: She told me to lock the door implies she decided; She reminded me to lock the door implies I had.
entries.transform: "Don't forget your passport." -> She reminded me to bring my passport.
examples: Please remind me to move the car before street cleaning.
The dentist's office reminds you twice, by text and by phone.
She reminded the committee that the vote had already been taken once.
He reminded us of the last time somebody tried this.
Nobody reminded me the clocks changed, and I sat in an empty room for an hour.
Let me remind you who signed the check.

entries.patterns: request + noun phrase / request + that-clause (subjunctive) / request + to-infinitive (the subject acts: requested to be reassigned) / request + sb + to-infinitive (formal and stiff; the passive is the natural home)
entries.never: request for a copy / request someone something
entries.meaning: A request lodged in a formal register, usually in writing. It is ask with the temperature dropped: nobody requests a glass of water from a friend.
entries.transform: "Please turn off all phones." -> The theater requested that all phones be turned off.
examples: He requested a copy of the inspection report in writing.
The court requested that both parties submit briefs by the tenth.
Guests are requested to keep noise down after ten.
She requested to be excused from the panel.
We request your presence at a reception following the ceremony.
The family has requested that donations go to the food bank instead of flowers.

entries.patterns: require + that-clause (subjunctive) / require + sb + to-infinitive / require + noun phrase / require + -ing (requires wearing a badge) / passive be required to (the commonest form of all)
entries.never: require that every visitor signs in / require someone doing something
entries.meaning: An obligation that comes from a rule, a policy, or the nature of the task rather than from a person's will. A person demands; a regulation requires. This is why require so often appears with an inanimate subject and in the passive: You are required to disclose it.
entries.transform: "Every visitor has to sign in." -> Policy requires that every visitor sign in. / Policy requires every visitor to sign in.
examples: The job requires you to be on call one weekend a month.
State law requires that landlords return deposits within twenty-one days.
The recipe requires buttermilk, and nothing else works the same way.
Employees are required to report outside income over five thousand dollars.
The grant requires filing a progress report every six months.
Nothing requires you to answer that question.

entries.patterns: stipulate + that-clause / stipulate + noun phrase / stipulate + wh-clause (stipulates how the money may be spent) / stipulate to + noun phrase (courtroom sense — see below)
entries.never: stipulate someone to do something
entries.meaning: A requirement written into an agreement as a precondition of it — the difference from require is that a stipulation is negotiated, part of a bargain, and usually on paper.
entries.transform: "The work has to be finished before we pay." -> The contract stipulates that the work be finished before payment.
examples: The will stipulates that the house not be sold for ten years.
Her contract stipulates a minimum of four weeks' notice.
The grant stipulates how much can go to overhead.
They stipulated that neither side would discuss the settlement publicly.
The rules stipulate that entries be submitted electronically.
Both parties stipulated to the timeline, which saved a day of testimony.

entries.patterns: summon + sb / summon + sb + to + noun phrase (summoned him to her office) / summon + sb + to-infinitive (summoned to appear) / summon + noun phrase (summoned help)
entries.never: summon someone that they come / summon to someone
entries.meaning: An order whose entire content is "come here" — the only verb in this group about location rather than action. The person summoned has no discretion; that is what distinguishes it from invite.
entries.transform: "Come to my office. Now." -> She summoned me to her office.
examples: The principal summoned both students to her office before lunch.
He was summoned to testify and took the Fifth.
She summoned the waiter with a look that took about a second.
The board was summoned into an emergency session on a Sunday.
Someone finally summoned help from the road above.
Being summoned to headquarters is never good news.

entries.type: reporting verb — command (also the general information verb)
entries.patterns: tell + sb + to-infinitive / tell + sb + that-clause / tell + sb + wh-clause / tell + sb + noun phrase (told me a story) / tell + sb + about + noun phrase
entries.never: tell to sit down / tell that he had left / say someone to do something
entries.meaning: The plainest directive verb in the language — force-neutral, register-neutral, and by far the most common. Everything more specific in this file is tell plus an attitude.
entries.transform: "Go home." -> He told me to go home.
examples: My boss told me to take the rest of the week off.
She told the kids not to open the door for anyone.
He told us that the flight had already been canceled.
Tell me what actually happened, not what's in the report.
Nobody told me the meeting had moved.
The sign tells you to stay on the trail, and people ignore it.

entries.patterns: urge + sb + to-infinitive / urge + that-clause (subjunctive) / urge + noun phrase (urged caution) / urge + sb + on (a different sense: urged the horse on)
entries.never: urge to someone to do something / urge someone doing something
entries.meaning: A recommendation delivered with urgency by someone with no power to compel. It is the exact midpoint of this file: stronger than advise, weaker than demand, and unlike either, it says the speaker cared about the outcome. Officials and editorial boards urge; that is nearly all they can do.
entries.transform: "You really need to see a doctor." -> She urged me to see a doctor.
examples: Her attorney urged her not to say anything publicly.
The Fed urged caution in a statement that moved nothing.
I'd urge you to read the dissent before making up your mind.
Public health officials urged residents to stay off the roads.
He urged that the matter be referred back to committee.
She urged me to apply, and I'm glad now that she did.
